title: Labor Watchdog Warns More H-1B and PERM Suspensions Are Coming
excerpt: Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said Friday that more colleges and companies will be cut off from the H-1B and PERM programmes as a fraud investigation widens — naming no institutions and giving no timetable.
body:
• The Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, warned on Friday, November 14 that more colleges and companies will be suspended from the H-1B visa and PERM labour certification programmes.
  • He named no institutions and gave no timetable. The warning extends a fraud investigation opened in July into alleged fraud and human trafficking in the two programmes.
  • In October, the department said it would stop accepting or processing PERM applications involving eight employers: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
  • If your employer is suspended, its new and pending PERM cases pause. Workers whose PERM was never filed have no basis under AC21 to extend H-1B status beyond six years with that employer.

The US Labor Department's internal watchdog has warned employers to expect more suspensions from the two programmes at the centre of skilled immigration to the United States.

In a video message released on Friday, Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said more colleges and companies would be cut off from the H-1B visa programme and the PERM labour certification programme, and that his office would keep investigating "as aggressive as we possibly can," according to US News Pulse's report of the message. He named no institutions and gave no timetable.

What PERM and H-1B suspensions actually do

The two programmes are sequential steps in most employment-based immigration. A PERM labour certification is the Labor Department's finding that no qualified US worker is available for a job and that hiring the foreign worker will not harm US wages and working conditions; most workers need an approved PERM before their employer can file the I-140 immigrant petition behind a green card. The H-1B is the temporary visa that lets the worker stay employed while that process runs.

A suspension of the kind announced in October is a pause, not a finding. Under the PERM regulation at 20 CFR 656.31(b), the department may suspend processing of an employer's applications while investigators examine possible fraud or willful misrepresentation, initially for up to 180 days, extendable by the National Certifying Officer, Wiiver's analysis of the rule explains. A debarment — a bar of one to three years — is a separate, formal penalty that requires a determination and appeal rights, and as of late October none of the eight companies appeared on the department's published debarment list.

How the campaign reached this point

The inspector general's office opened a nationwide investigation in July into alleged fraud and human trafficking in the H-1B and PERM systems, and is working with the White House Fraud Task Force led by Vice President JD Vance. In May, the department's Office of Foreign Labor Certification suspended processing of Cloudera's PERM applications for 180 days, citing a Justice Department lawsuit. On October 8, at a White House press conference, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department would not accept new PERM applications, or process pending ones, involving Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini, citing ongoing investigations.

Details remain thin on the public record. Ashoori Law's analysis notes that as of October 30 the department had published no news release, OFLC announcement or Federal Register notice setting out the October action's written terms, and that the allegations behind it are not findings of fraud.

What this means if you are in the system

A suspension at your employer does not cancel existing H-1B approvals, previously certified PERMs or approved I-140 petitions, based on what officials announced in October. What it pauses is that employer's PERM pipeline: new filings are not accepted and pending ones are not processed while the suspension runs.

The sharpest exposure is timing. A certified PERM still expires after 180 days under 20 CFR 656.30(b), even during a suspension. And H-1B workers approaching the six-year limit generally extend beyond it under the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) on the basis of a pending or approved PERM or I-140; a worker whose PERM was never filed has no such basis with a suspended employer. Workers at the eight named employers — and at any institution named next — should confirm their case posture with their employer's immigration counsel before making job or travel decisions.

What to watch

D'Esposito's warning signals the next names will come from the same investigation, and that colleges are now explicitly in scope alongside companies. Whether the department publishes written terms for the suspensions — the document immigration lawyers have been waiting for since October — will decide how much certainty affected workers get about end dates and appeal rights.
